## Example 3.20 {#fv5-example-3-20 .fv-lesson .intersection-lesson }

```{=html}
<p class="inter-source">2026 Kambala Mathematics Extension 2 Task 2, Q7(b)(i) · 3 marks</p><p>Consider the point <span data-math="A(4,2,5)"></span> and the line <span data-math="\ell"></span> with vector equation</p><div class="fv-equation"><span data-math="\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-2\\2\\4\end{bmatrix}."></span></div><p>Find the minimum distance between the point <span data-math="A"></span> and the line <span data-math="\ell"></span>.</p>
```

<div class="booklet-cue">Booklet Example 3.20 · p. 67</div>

::: {.notes}
Preserve the booklet question and its label A. Work the example in OneNote; both methods use B=(1,2,3), d=(−2,2,4), u=BA=(3,0,2). Thus u·d=2 and d·d=24.

Method 1 — projection. BH=proj_d u=(2/24)d=(−1/6,1/6,1/3). HA=BA−BH=(19/6,−1/6,5/3). Minimum distance |HA|=sqrt(361/36+1/36+25/9)=sqrt(77/6)=sqrt(462)/6. Suggested, not official, 3-mark guide: 1 mark for the joining vector and its projection; 1 mark for the perpendicular remainder; 1 mark for its exact magnitude.

Method 2 — perpendicularity. P(t)=(1−2t,2+2t,3+4t), so PA=u−td=(3+2t,−2t,2−4t). Require PA·d=−6−4t−4t+8−16t=2−24t=0, hence t=1/12. H=(5/6,13/6,10/3) and HA=(19/6,−1/6,5/3), giving the same minimum distance sqrt(462)/6. Suggested, not official, 3-mark guide: 1 mark for PA and the perpendicularity condition; 1 mark for t and the corresponding joining vector or foot; 1 mark for the exact minimum distance.

Optional calculus alternative: D²(t)=(3+2t)²+(−2t)²+(2−4t)²=24t²−4t+13. Its derivative 48t−4 is zero at t=1/12; the positive quadratic coefficient establishes the minimum. D²(1/12)=77/6. This agrees with projection and perpendicularity. Keep this in notes unless useful for a student question.
:::
